736552d44b416487bd54171a.title: GCSE results: girls still ahead but gender gap narrows as hundreds of thousands of pupils receive grades – as it happened
736552d44b416487bd54171a.author: Mabel Banfield-Nwachi; Taz Ali; Tom Ambrose; Sally Weale; Richard Adams
736552d44b416487bd54171a.content:
The proportion of GCSE students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland achieving at least a grade 4 (equivalent to a C) has fallen slightly this year, to 67.3% from 67.4% in 2025. This is the same as the proportion recorded in 2019, before the pandemic.
While it is a minor decrease, it still means nearly a third of teenagers are not achieving basic English and maths skills when finishing school. In England, students who fail to reach a grade 4 or equivalent in English or maths GCSEs have to retake them.
More students aged 17 and above took English and maths this year, likely due to the resits policy in England. But results show the pass rate has worsened for this cohort, falling by 1.4 percentage points for English and 1.7 for maths compared with last year.
That’s all from us on the GCSE results live blog today, thanks for following along.
Here are the main developments from today:
The proportion of GCSE students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland achieving at least a grade 4 (equivalent to a C) has fallen slightly this year, to 67.3% from 67.4% in 2025. This is the same as the proportion recorded in 2019, before the pandemic.
The overall results for 16-year-olds in England nudged slightly higher compared with last year, with the proportion receiving grades 7, 8 and 9 – equivalent to grades A and A* – rising by 0.1 of a percentage point to 23.1%.
The proportion of nearly 700,000 16-year-olds in England who got a grade 4 (equivalent to a C) or better also rose to 70.7%, compared with 70.5% in 2025.
Pupils collect their GCSE results at Egglescliffe School, in Eaglescliffe, North Yorkshire. Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PA
Girls continue to outperform boys at GCSE, but the gap is narrowing. Almost a fifth (19.6%) of boys’ GCSE entries in England, Wales and Northern Ireland were awarded a grade 7 or higher (equivalent to an A) compared with nearly a quarter (24.4%) of girls’ entries, a 4.8 percentage point gap, down from 5.1 last year. Overall, 70.2% of girls achieved a pass rate (grade 4 and higher) compared with 64.4% of boys, a 5.8 percentage point gap, a decrease from 6.2 last year.
In England, London remains on top for pupils achieving a grade 7 or above, at 28.6%. This is a slight increase from last year, when 28.4% of GCSE students in the capital achieved the top grades. North-east England had the lowest figure, with 17.7% of GCSE entries awarded at least a 7, down from 17.8% in 2025.
In a message to students, prime minister Andy Burnham said the government is creating “more opportunities” for young people to “choose the path that’s right for them”. He added: “Whatever your results, remember there isn’t just one route to success.”
Education secretary Lucy Powell said the government is looking at changing the resits policy in England, noting that only one in five students who resit English and maths were passing them. “For some, they’re doing it many times over,” she added. “So we’re branding them a failure after failure after failure. It’s knocking their confidence.
Among those celebrating their GCSE results today were quadruplets Ellen, Eric, Layla, and Rose Lamb, who all attended Aureus School in Didcot, Oxfordshire.
Quadruplets Rose, Eric, Layla and Ellen Lamb receive their GCSE results at Aureus School in Didcot, Oxfordshire. Photograph: David Collins Photography
Ellen achieved one grade 9, five grade 8s, three grade 7s, and one grade 6. She is heading to Oxford City College to study A-levels in biology, chemistry and maths and hopes to become a paediatrician.
“I’ve really enjoyed the sense of community at Aureus,” she said. “The teachers have always been incredibly supportive, and encouraged me to challenge myself both academically and personally.
“Some of my favourite memories include our Year 11 prom, taking part in the school production, and celebrating after completing our GCSE exams.”
Eric is going on to study dance, while Layla will be studying English, history and psychology at sixth form and Rose will study history, sociology, and English A-levels.
Gender and golf course studies are examples of “Mickey Mouse” degrees, Suella Braverman has said.
Asked to name a specific degree which falls under Reform UK’s definition of a “Mickey Mouse” course that should be avoided, the party’s education spokesperson said:
In terms of Mickey Mouse courses, listen, this has been well-chronicled for many years. Whether it’s gender studies, whether it’s golf course studies, I think I’ve seen there’s not a necessity. There’s not a value in many of these degrees.
Now I know that might be uncomfortable to those people who have those qualifications, but the reality is you’ve got to ask yourself: what are your graduate outcomes looking like?
Have you really spent three years of your life in the best possible way, and was it worth £50,000 worth of debt.
Young people are coming out of university unable to get on to the housing ladder, unable and unwilling to get married, unable to start a family. Why? Because they’re starting off with their hands behind their backs because they’ve been sold a line that university is the pathway to success.
Reform: don't waste time 'studying for a pointless degree at a mediocre university'
Tom Ambrose
Suella Braverman has urged young people getting their GCSE results not to “waste your time studying for a pointless degree at a mediocre university”.
The Reform UK education spokesperson made the comment as she set out the party’s plans to create 600,000 more apprenticeship starts a year by the end of the first term of a Reform government.
Suella Braverman during a Reform UK Press Conference in Enfield, London. Photograph: Andy Rain/EPA
As she set out the policy, Braverman addressed students receiving their exam results, telling them:
My advice to those young people today getting their results, my advice to those grandparents and those parents looking at the young people in their families who may be getting their results today: Be careful, don’t get ripped off by the great university scam.
Don’t waste your time studying for a pointless degree at a mediocre university. If you want to work hard, if you want to move forward, earn a wage, and have opportunities in your life, take up and look for apprentices.
And a Reform UK government will ensure that those opportunities exist. Your success is our country’s success. We’re on your side, and when I said I wanted a skills revolution, I meant it.”
For more UK politics news, follow our live blog here:
Chris Zarraga, director of Schools North East which represents 1,150 schools in the regions, said there was some “genuinely encouraging news” in today’s results.
At grade 4 and above, the gap between the north-east and London has narrowed and is back to around where it was before the pandemic.
But the picture at the highest grades remains concerning. The gap at grades 7 to 9 has increased again this year and remains wider than it was in 2019.
The movement each year might look relatively small, but the important point is its persistence. Year after year, this divide remains; and is then reflected in student destinations, employment rates, and HE progression rates.
We have to understand what these figures are telling us. There is not a north-south divide in the quality of schools, nor in the talent, potential or aspirations of young people.
There is a structural divide in the circumstances and opportunities surrounding them.
Schools in the north-east are working incredibly hard to overcome those circumstances.
But schools cannot independently fix poverty, stretched public services, shortages in special educational needs and disabilities (Send) support, transport barriers, unequal access to enrichment or very different local economic opportunities.
These inequalities are neither inevitable nor acceptable. The government needs to treat them as a system challenge and address the conditions around schools as well as what happens inside them.”
PA has reported a heartwarming story about a Sudanese refugee who passed his GCSEs in English and maths.
Nasser Hamid, 20, of Ipswich, achieved grade 4 in both subjects, collecting his maths results today after having passed English earlier this year.
He studies at Suffolk New College, where he is also taking an IT course.
On finding out he now has his English and maths qualifications, he said: “I feel proud – it is one of the proudest moments in my life – this is the result I was waiting for to step forward.
“Thanks to Suffolk New College, without their help I wouldn’t be standing here.”
Nasser Hamid, a student who fled war-torn Sudan to live in the UK, said that passing his GCSE exams in maths and English is ‘one of the proudest moments in my life’. Photograph: Suffolk New College/PA
Nasser is an aspiring football referee, after an injury ended his dream of being a professional player. He recently oversaw a charity football match at Ipswich Town’s ground, Portman Road, and said he would love to referee at a future World Cup.
He also officiates at Saturday and Sunday league games.
He urged others in a similar position to “just believe in yourself”.
“With discipline and hard work, you can achieve your goals,” he said.
Nasser said he was “pushing forward to be an engineer”.
“I’m on track,” he said.
“Next, I’m going to do an access course and then (hopefully) go to university to study engineering.”
David Squire, head of maths at Suffolk New College, said: “I’ve never been prouder of a learner in my life.”
On subject choice, statistics and business studies may have grown in popularity this year – up 11% and 8% respectively – but computing has dipped 7%. Myles McGinley, managing director of Cambridge OCR, explained: “The emergence of AI could be leading to students thinking they don’t need to know how to code.
“But I would say maybe that’s something that would be up for debate. I think potentially computer science is more important than ever in the age of AI.
“And while vibe coding might be all the rage, I think AI won’t be able to replace a solid understanding of how software works, how technology can solve real-world problems and how it can create a good user experience.”
One of the key areas of concern following today’s GCSE results will be the high failure rates for those students in England forced to resit English and maths GCSE after previously failing to secure a pass at the age of 16.
It is a longstanding problem and the government has already proposed the introduction of a “stepping stone” qualification to help better prepare students who are struggling but frustrated school leaders said more fundamental change is needed.
Paul Whiteman, general secretary of the NAHT school leaders’ union, said: “We have long called for an end to the current policy which forces students into dispiriting rounds of repeated, demotivating resits.
“The curriculum review focus was on ensuring students are better prepared for resits and introducing a stepping stone qualification.
“Today’s data shows why more fundamental changes to this policy are needed, with only 18.8% of students aged 17 and over achieving a grade 4 in English, and 13.6% of students achieving a grade 4 in maths – both down on last year, when these figures were 19.7% and 15.3% respectively.
Pupils celebrate their GCSE results at
Leeds Grammar School, in Leeds, Yorkshire. Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PA
“What is needed are more appropriate and engaging alternatives to GCSEs in English and maths at key stage 4 which enable students to study for qualifications that better suit their needs and aspirations.”
Girls continue to outperform boys at GCSE, but the gap is closing and is now 2.9 percentage points (pp) lower than it was in 2019. Richard Harry, executive director of qualifications and assessment at the Welsh exam board WJEC, urged caution however.
“The gap is only very slightly narrower this year – it’s a very small change,” he said. “I think it would be difficult to speculate too much around the differences for such small changes.”
Concern will also focus on persistent regional differences, with London once again the highest performing area with 28.6% of grades 7 and above, up 0.2pp from last year. In the north-east, the lowest performing region, 17.7% of grades awarded were 7 and above, down 0.1pp from last year.
Carl Cullinane, director of research and policy at the Sutton Trust education charity, said there had been “no progress” in addressing regional imbalances in GCSE performance, with the gap between London and the rest of the country continuing to grow.
“Forthcoming curriculum and assessment reforms, and future government spending decisions, must have a laser focus on closing gaps in attainment and progression across the country.”
The Sutton Trust also pointed out that the gap between state comprehensives and private school pupils getting the top grades may have narrowed slightly by 0.9pp, but it remains vast at 27pp.
London widens lead over other regions for top grades
Looking at the results in England on a regional level, London remains on top for pupils achieving a grade 7 or above, at 28.6%.
This is a slight increase from last year, when 28.4% of GCSE students in the capital achieved the top grades.
North-east England had the lowest figure, with 17.7% of GCSE entries awarded at least a 7, down from 17.8% in 2025.
This means the regional gap has widened between the highest and lowest proportions of pupils achieving a grade 7 or above, from 10.6 percentage points last year to 10.9 points this year. It is the largest gap since the start of available data in 2010, according to analysis by PA.
Here’s what the data says about the other regions:
North-west England: 18.9% of entries received a grade 7 or above, up slightly from 18.8% in 2025.
London – north-west gap: The gap widened to 9.7 percentage points, from 9.6 in 2025, close to the recent record of 9.9 points in 2024.
East Midlands: 18.2% of entries received a grade 7 or above, 10.4 percentage points behind London, up from 10.3 in 2025.
West Midlands: 18.3% of entries received a grade 7 or above, 10.3 percentage points behind London, up from 9.9 in 2025.
Wider regional divide: The gap between London and both the East and West Midlands has widened to its largest level since at least 2010.
Here some pictures on the newswires of students picking up their GCSE results today:
Prosper Okoroafor (centre) at the Ark Greenwich Free School, Woolwich, south London. Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PA
Farzana Fatimah reacts as she reads her GCSE results with her mother at Plashet City of London Academy. Photograph: Carl Court/Getty Images
Ethan Rillon celebrates his GCSE results with his sister Angela Rillon (left) and his mother, Jan Rillon, at Hazelwood Intergrated College in Newtownabbey, North Belfast. Photograph: Mark Marlow/PA
Iris Hamilton-Potter and friend Poppy Plant receive their GCSE results at Llanishen High School in Cardiff, Wales. Photograph: Matthew Horwood/Getty Images
Education secretary Lucy Powell speaks with students collecting their GCSE results at Harper Green School in Farnworth, Bolton. Photograph: Peter Byrne/PA
Ellie Anns, Isabella Bruce, Izzy Phillips, Belle Bosham, Susanna Dat and Luci Tedeschi at St Gabriel's School in Newbury, Berkshire. Photograph: David Hartley/Shutterstock
The gap in GCSE results between boys and girls in England, Wales and Northern Ireland has shrunk again this year.
Almost a fifth (19.6%) of boys’ GCSE entries were awarded a grade 7 or higher (equivalent to an A) compared with nearly a quarter (24.4%) of girls’ entries, a 4.8 percentage point gap, down from 5.1 last year.
Overall, 70.2% of girls achieved a pass rate (grade 4 and higher) compared with 64.4% of boys, a 5.8 percentage point gap, a decrease from 6.2 last year.
These are the narrowest leads enjoyed by girls since at least 2000, which is the earliest archive data available, PA reported.
The proportion of GCSE students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland achieving at least a grade 4 (equivalent to a C) has fallen slightly this year, to 67.3% from 67.4% in 2025. This is the same as the proportion recorded in 2019, before the pandemic.
While it is a minor decrease, it still means nearly a third of teenagers are not achieving basic English and maths skills when finishing school. In England, students who fail to reach a grade 4 or equivalent in English or maths GCSEs have to retake them.
More students aged 17 and above took English and maths this year, likely due to the resits policy in England. But results show the pass rate has worsened for this cohort, falling by 1.4 percentage points for English and 1.7 for maths compared with last year.
'Concerning' fall in language GCSE entries, says British Academy
The British Academy, the national organisation for humanities and social sciences, said its analysis of GCSE results today shows business and psychology are up but languages face another year of decline.
Among its key findings were:
French seeing its sharpest fall since 2018, with a 5.4% decrease in take-up this year.
Other modern languages, which includes Arabic, Chinese and Urdu among others,are also down by 4%.
Spanish growth may be slowing down, with a 0.3% increase compared to 2.6% last year and 6.2% the year before.
German is up 0.2%, a very small increase compared to its long-term decline of 12.5% over the past 5 years.
The highest growing subjects in Shape (the acronym for social sciences, humanities and arts) was business studies, with a 7.9% increase.
Sociology and psychology continue to rise, by 4.8% and 3% respectively.
Susan Smith, president of the British Academy, said: “This year’s GCSE entries show that young people continue to be inspired by subjects providing insight into people, economy and society.
The growth of business studies, sociology and psychology, in particular, show increasing appetite for skills nurtured by the social sciences, arts and humanities."
However, the continued fall in language entries is concerning. Languages are vital for diplomacy, trade and cultural understanding. AI translation is no match for the human communications skills and capabilities we need to navigate an increasingly interconnected, but divided and volatile world. Yet, losing languages at this level has a domino effect across the entire education system, and once this expertise disappears, it will be very hard to recover.
As government reflects on future education pathways, we urge ministers to seize every opportunity to give all young people access to a broad, balanced curriculum, delivering the critical thinking and creativity that employers value and the UK needs.”
Here are some statements from the prime minister and the education secretary on the GSCE results today.
Andy Burnham said:
Congratulations to everyone collecting their results today, you should be proud of the hard work that got you here.
Whether the next step is sixth form, a college course, an apprenticeship, a T Level, work, or something else entirely, we’re ensuring that there are more opportunities than ever to choose your own path to get on in life. I’m determined to bring back hope and give every young person the chance to fulfil their potential.
Lucy Powell said:
Massive congratulations to everyone collecting their results today – be proud of what it took to get here, and thank you to the teachers and families who backed you every step of the way.
More of you are hitting top grades in maths, and technical pass rates are climbing in every region. That’s proof there is no wrong door, only different routes that suit everyone’s individual ambition.
But there’s more to do to put academic and technical qualifications on an equal footing, so we’re introducing V Levels and expanding T Levels and apprenticeships, so wherever you’re headed next, there’s a path that works for you.”
Andy Burnham and Lucy Powell speaking to apprentices at the Alstom factory in Derby. Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/AFP/Getty Images
736552d44b416487bd54171a.summary: Hundreds of thousands of pupils across England, Wales, and Northern Ireland received their GCSE results, with the overall pass rate falling slightly to 67.3%. Girls continue to outperform boys, though the gender performance gap has narrowed slightly compared to previous years. Meanwhile, education leaders have raised concerns over declining pass rates and high failure figures for older students required to retake English and maths exams.
key_points: The proportion of students achieving at least a grade 4 dropped slightly to 67.3%, matching pre-pandemic levels from 2019.
Girls continue to outperform boys, though the attainment gap between genders has decreased.
Pass rates for students aged 17 and over retaking English and maths worsened, falling by 1.4 and 1.7 percentage points respectively.
London remained the top-performing region for top grades (7 and above), while the north-east recorded the lowest figure.

In terms of Mickey Mouse courses, listen, this has been well-chronicled for many years. Whether it’s gender studies, whether it’s golf course studies, I think I’ve seen there’s not a necessity. There’s not a value in many of these degrees.
Now I know that might be uncomfortable to those people who have those qualifications, but the reality is you’ve got to ask yourself: what are your graduate outcomes looking like?
Have you really spent three years of your life in the best possible way, and was it worth £50,000 worth of debt.
Young people are coming out of university unable to get on to the housing ladder, unable and unwilling to get married, unable to start a family. Why? Because they’re starting off with their hands behind their backs because they’ve been sold a line that university is the pathway to success.
Reform: don't waste time 'studying for a pointless degree at a mediocre university'
Tom Ambrose
Suella Braverman has urged young people getting their GCSE results not to “waste your time studying for a pointless degree at a mediocre university”.
The Reform UK education spokesperson made the comment as she set out the party’s plans to create 600,000 more apprenticeship starts a year by the end of the first term of a Reform government.
Suella Braverman during a Reform UK Press Conference in Enfield, London. Photograph: Andy Rain/EPA
As she set out the policy, Braverman addressed students receiving their exam results, telling them:
My advice to those young people today getting their results, my advice to those grandparents and those parents looking at the young people in their families who may be getting their results today: Be careful, don’t get ripped off by the great university scam.
Don’t waste your time studying for a pointless degree at a mediocre university. If you want to work hard, if you want to move forward, earn a wage, and have opportunities in your life, take up and look for apprentices.
And a Reform UK government will ensure that those opportunities exist. Your success is our country’s success. We’re on your side, and when I said I wanted a skills revolution, I meant it.”
For more UK politics news, follow our live blog here:
Chris Zarraga, director of Schools North East which represents 1,150 schools in the regions, said there was some “genuinely encouraging news” in today’s results.
At grade 4 and above, the gap between the north-east and London has narrowed and is back to around where it was before the pandemic.
But the picture at the highest grades remains concerning. The gap at grades 7 to 9 has increased again this year and remains wider than it was in 2019.
The movement each year might look relatively small, but the important point is its persistence. Year after year, this divide remains; and is then reflected in student destinations, employment rates, and HE progression rates.
We have to understand what these figures are telling us. There is not a north-south divide in the quality of schools, nor in the talent, potential or aspirations of young people.
There is a structural divide in the circumstances and opportunities surrounding them.
Schools in the north-east are working incredibly hard to overcome those circumstances.
But schools cannot independently fix poverty, stretched public services, shortages in special educational needs and disabilities (Send) support, transport barriers, unequal access to enrichment or very different local economic opportunities.
These inequalities are neither inevitable nor acceptable. The government needs to treat them as a system challenge and address the conditions around schools as well as what happens inside them.”
PA has reported a heartwarming story about a Sudanese refugee who passed his GCSEs in English and maths.
Nasser Hamid, 20, of Ipswich, achieved grade 4 in both subjects, collecting his maths results today after having passed English earlier this year.
He studies at Suffolk New College, where he is also taking an IT course.
On finding out he now has his English and maths qualifications, he said: “I feel proud – it is one of the proudest moments in my life – this is the result I was waiting for to step forward.
“Thanks to Suffolk New College, without their help I wouldn’t be standing here.”
Nasser Hamid, a student who fled war-torn Sudan to live in the UK, said that passing his GCSE exams in maths and English is ‘one of the proudest moments in my life’. Photograph: Suffolk New College/PA
Nasser is an aspiring football referee, after an injury ended his dream of being a professional player. He recently oversaw a charity football match at Ipswich Town’s ground, Portman Road, and said he would love to referee at a future World Cup.
He also officiates at Saturday and Sunday league games.
He urged others in a similar position to “just believe in yourself”.
“With discipline and hard work, you can achieve your goals,” he said.
Nasser said he was “pushing forward to be an engineer”.
“I’m on track,” he said.
“Next, I’m going to do an access course and then (hopefully) go to university to study engineering.”
David Squire, head of maths at Suffolk New College, said: “I’ve never been prouder of a learner in my life.”
On subject choice, statistics and business studies may have grown in popularity this year – up 11% and 8% respectively – but computing has dipped 7%. Myles McGinley, managing director of Cambridge OCR, explained: “The emergence of AI could be leading to students thinking they don’t need to know how to code.
“But I would say maybe that’s something that would be up for debate. I think potentially computer science is more important than ever in the age of AI.
“And while vibe coding might be all the rage, I think AI won’t be able to replace a solid understanding of how software works, how technology can solve real-world problems and how it can create a good user experience.”
One of the key areas of concern following today’s GCSE results will be the high failure rates for those students in England forced to resit English and maths GCSE after previously failing to secure a pass at the age of 16.
It is a longstanding problem and the government has already proposed the introduction of a “stepping stone” qualification to help better prepare students who are struggling but frustrated school leaders said more fundamental change is needed.
Paul Whiteman, general secretary of the NAHT school leaders’ union, said: “We have long called for an end to the current policy which forces students into dispiriting rounds of repeated, demotivating resits.
“The curriculum review focus was on ensuring students are better prepared for resits and introducing a stepping stone qualification.
“Today’s data shows why more fundamental changes to this policy are needed, with only 18.8% of students aged 17 and over achieving a grade 4 in English, and 13.6% of students achieving a grade 4 in maths – both down on last year, when these figures were 19.7% and 15.3% respectively.
Pupils celebrate their GCSE results at
Leeds Grammar School, in Leeds, Yorkshire. Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PA
“What is needed are more appropriate and engaging alternatives to GCSEs in English and maths at key stage 4 which enable students to study for qualifications that better suit their needs and aspirations.”
Girls continue to outperform boys at GCSE, but the gap is closing and is now 2.9 percentage points (pp) lower than it was in 2019. Richard Harry, executive director of qualifications and assessment at the Welsh exam board WJEC, urged caution however.
“The gap is only very slightly narrower this year – it’s a very small change,” he said. “I think it would be difficult to speculate too much around the differences for such small changes.”
Concern will also focus on persistent regional differences, with London once again the highest performing area with 28.6% of grades 7 and above, up 0.2pp from last year. In the north-east, the lowest performing region, 17.7% of grades awarded were 7 and above, down 0.1pp from last year.
Carl Cullinane, director of research and policy at the Sutton Trust education charity, said there had been “no progress” in addressing regional imbalances in GCSE performance, with the gap between London and the rest of the country continuing to grow.
“Forthcoming curriculum and assessment reforms, and future government spending decisions, must have a laser focus on closing gaps in attainment and progression across the country.”
The Sutton Trust also pointed out that the gap between state comprehensives and private school pupils getting the top grades may have narrowed slightly by 0.9pp, but it remains vast at 27pp.
London widens lead over other regions for top grades
Looking at the results in England on a regional level, London remains on top for pupils achieving a grade 7 or above, at 28.6%.
This is a slight increase from last year, when 28.4% of GCSE students in the capital achieved the top grades.
North-east England had the lowest figure, with 17.7% of GCSE entries awarded at least a 7, down from 17.8% in 2025.
This means the regional gap has widened between the highest and lowest proportions of pupils achieving a grade 7 or above, from 10.6 percentage points last year to 10.9 points this year. It is the largest gap since the start of available data in 2010, according to analysis by PA.
Here’s what the data says about the other regions:
North-west England: 18.9% of entries received a grade 7 or above, up slightly from 18.8% in 2025.
London – north-west gap: The gap widened to 9.7 percentage points, from 9.6 in 2025, close to the recent record of 9.9 points in 2024.
East Midlands: 18.2% of entries received a grade 7 or above, 10.4 percentage points behind London, up from 10.3 in 2025.
West Midlands: 18.3% of entries received a grade 7 or above, 10.3 percentage points behind London, up from 9.9 in 2025.
Wider regional divide: The gap between London and both the East and West Midlands has widened to its largest level since at least 2010.
Here some pictures on the newswires of students picking up their GCSE results today:
Prosper Okoroafor (centre) at the Ark Greenwich Free School, Woolwich, south London. Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PA
Farzana Fatimah reacts as she reads her GCSE results with her mother at Plashet City of London Academy. Photograph: Carl Court/Getty Images
Ethan Rillon celebrates his GCSE results with his sister Angela Rillon (left) and his mother, Jan Rillon, at Hazelwood Intergrated College in Newtownabbey, North Belfast. Photograph: Mark Marlow/PA
Iris Hamilton-Potter and friend Poppy Plant receive their GCSE results at Llanishen High School in Cardiff, Wales. Photograph: Matthew Horwood/Getty Images
Education secretary Lucy Powell speaks with students collecting their GCSE results at Harper Green School in Farnworth, Bolton. Photograph: Peter Byrne/PA
Ellie Anns, Isabella Bruce, Izzy Phillips, Belle Bosham, Susanna Dat and Luci Tedeschi at St Gabriel's School in Newbury, Berkshire. Photograph: David Hartley/Shutterstock
The gap in GCSE results between boys and girls in England, Wales and Northern Ireland has shrunk again this year.
Almost a fifth (19.6%) of boys’ GCSE entries were awarded a grade 7 or higher (equivalent to an A) compared with nearly a quarter (24.4%) of girls’ entries, a 4.8 percentage point gap, down from 5.1 last year.
Overall, 70.2% of girls achieved a pass rate (grade 4 and higher) compared with 64.4% of boys, a 5.8 percentage point gap, a decrease from 6.2 last year.
These are the narrowest leads enjoyed by girls since at least 2000, which is the earliest archive data available, PA reported.
The proportion of GCSE students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland achieving at least a grade 4 (equivalent to a C) has fallen slightly this year, to 67.3% from 67.4% in 2025. This is the same as the proportion recorded in 2019, before the pandemic.
While it is a minor decrease, it still means nearly a third of teenagers are not achieving basic English and maths skills when finishing school. In England, students who fail to reach a grade 4 or equivalent in English or maths GCSEs have to retake them.
More students aged 17 and above took English and maths this year, likely due to the resits policy in England. But results show the pass rate has worsened for this cohort, falling by 1.4 percentage points for English and 1.7 for maths compared with last year.
'Concerning' fall in language GCSE entries, says British Academy
The British Academy, the national organisation for humanities and social sciences, said its analysis of GCSE results today shows business and psychology are up but languages face another year of decline.
Among its key findings were:
French seeing its sharpest fall since 2018, with a 5.4% decrease in take-up this year.
Other modern languages, which includes Arabic, Chinese and Urdu among others,are also down by 4%.
Spanish growth may be slowing down, with a 0.3% increase compared to 2.6% last year and 6.2% the year before.
German is up 0.2%, a very small increase compared to its long-term decline of 12.5% over the past 5 years.
The highest growing subjects in Shape (the acronym for social sciences, humanities and arts) was business studies, with a 7.9% increase.
Sociology and psychology continue to rise, by 4.8% and 3% respectively.
Susan Smith, president of the British Academy, said: “This year’s GCSE entries show that young people continue to be inspired by subjects providing insight into people, economy and society.
The growth of business studies, sociology and psychology, in particular, show increasing appetite for skills nurtured by the social sciences, arts and humanities."
However, the continued fall in language entries is concerning. Languages are vital for diplomacy, trade and cultural understanding. AI translation is no match for the human communications skills and capabilities we need to navigate an increasingly interconnected, but divided and volatile world. Yet, losing languages at this level has a domino effect across the entire education system, and once this expertise disappears, it will be very hard to recover.
As government reflects on future education pathways, we urge ministers to seize every opportunity to give all young people access to a broad, balanced curriculum, delivering the critical thinking and creativity that employers value and the UK needs.”
Here are some statements from the prime minister and the education secretary on the GSCE results today.
Andy Burnham said:
Congratulations to everyone collecting their results today, you should be proud of the hard work that got you here.
Whether the next step is sixth form, a college course, an apprenticeship, a T Level, work, or something else entirely, we’re ensuring that there are more opportunities than ever to choose your own path to get on in life. I’m determined to bring back hope and give every young person the chance to fulfil their potential.
Lucy Powell said:
Massive congratulations to everyone collecting their results today – be proud of what it took to get here, and thank you to the teachers and families who backed you every step of the way.
More of you are hitting top grades in maths, and technical pass rates are climbing in every region. That’s proof there is no wrong door, only different routes that suit everyone’s individual ambition.
But there’s more to do to put academic and technical qualifications on an equal footing, so we’re introducing V Levels and expanding T Levels and apprenticeships, so wherever you’re headed next, there’s a path that works for you.”
Andy Burnham and Lucy Powell speaking to apprentices at the Alstom factory in Derby. Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/AFP/Getty Images
2f9a189daaaaf4aad0684eaa.summary: Hundreds of thousands of pupils across England, Wales, and Northern Ireland received their GCSE results, with the overall pass rate falling slightly to 67.3%. Girls continue to outperform boys, though the gender performance gap has narrowed slightly compared to previous years. Meanwhile, education leaders have raised concerns over declining pass rates and high failure figures for older students required to retake English and maths exams.
key_points: The proportion of students achieving at least a grade 4 dropped slightly to 67.3%, matching pre-pandemic levels from 2019.
Girls continue to outperform boys, though the attainment gap between genders has decreased.
Pass rates for students aged 17 and over retaking English and maths worsened, falling by 1.4 and 1.7 percentage points respectively.
London remained the top-performing region for top grades (7 and above), while the north-east recorded the lowest figure.

cfea4d5828da54ff4e19226e.title: Tourists flee as smugglers drop dozens of migrants on Spanish beach
cfea4d5828da54ff4e19226e.author: Graham Keeley
cfea4d5828da54ff4e19226e.content:
Dozens of migrants stormed a beach in the south of Spain and caused tourists to flee on Wednesday.
More than 60 migrants jumped from a speedboat onto the beach, prompting tourists to pack up their things and leave. Some people on the beach were seen calling the police.
Before many of the migrants could even reach the beach, two men driving the vessel – a high-speed launch – turned it round and headed back out to the Mediterranean.
Migrants were seen leaping from the vessel into the water, before swimming ashore and walking past the sunbathers towards the nearby town of Atamaría in Murcia.
The incident happened at about 1pm on Wednesday at the secluded Cala del Barco near the La Manga resort in Murcia.
La Manga is known for its golf courses and football training facilities, which have been used by teams including the England national side and more recently Arsenal and Newcastle.
Francisco Bernabé, a conservative senator from the nearby town of La Unión, said in a social media post: “Dozens of illegal migrants today at La Manga cove.
“Why was it not possible to detect a vessel of those dimensions with all radars before? Are they broken? Do they have them turned off? Or are they working and they simply ignore them?”
‘This cannot be normalised’
Noelia Arroyo, the mayor of the nearby port city of Cartagena, told Cadena Ser radio: “This cannot be normalised.
“If a migrant can reach a cove like this, disembark in full view of citizens and leave, we have to ask ourselves how the control of our maritime borders is working?”
Spain’s civil guard later said they had arrested 45 men, two women and 15 boys. All were healthy, said the Red Cross. The migrants were handed over to Spain’s National Police, which deals with migration issues.
Most will be returned to their country of origin, but if they do claim asylum, they will undergo a lengthy process to evaluate their claims.
This is the latest incident of migrants being dropped off by traffickers on beaches after travelling at high speeds across the Mediterranean from Morocco or Algeria to Spain.
cfea4d5828da54ff4e19226e.summary: Dozens of migrants arrived on a beach in southern Spain after being dropped off by traffickers on a high-speed vessel, causing tourists to flee. Spanish authorities subsequently arrested 45 men, two women, and 15 boys, all of whom were reported to be healthy. Local officials criticized the apparent lack of maritime border detection following the midday incident.
key_points: More than 60 migrants jumped from a speedboat onto Cala del Barco beach in Murcia on Wednesday.
The incident caused tourists to pack up and leave while some called the police.
Spain's civil guard arrested 45 men, two women, and 15 boys.
Local officials questioned the effectiveness of maritime border controls after the event.

1040d48b1f6da54005a3a79b.title: Sales of trainers dive at JD Sports as cost of living pressures bite
1040d48b1f6da54005a3a79b.author: Kalyeena Makortoff
1040d48b1f6da54005a3a79b.content:
The sports fashion retailer JD has cut its profit forecasts as cost of living pressures, fuelled by the US war on Iran, weighed on sales of trainers.
JD Sports, which sells brands including Nike and Adidas, said widespread inflation had hit shoppers’ wallets, resulting in a drop in sales across important markets such as the US, where it struggled to shift trainers and other footwear.
Bosses went on to warn that the wider fall in consumer spending was likely to continue into the second half of the year, leading to lower-than-expected profits. The retailer now expects pre-tax profits of between £700m and £800m for the full year, having previously hoped to reach £750m to £850m.
The news led to a 12% drop in JD’s London-listed shares on Thursday morning to their lowest level since July.
Régis Schultz, chief executive, said: “Trading in the second quarter remained tough,” t adding that the company had been forced to cut prices and offer promotional sales to compensate, as “our core consumer was impacted by incremental cost of living pressures.”
![Adidas, Nike and New Balance shoes at a newly renovated JD Sports store at Westfield Stratford, London.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/ed5a17474bca3a3ac752e4b6d037ac2e589a3c3c/593_0_5028_4022/master/5028.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The company, which runs 4,800 stores worldwide including the JD, Blacks and Millets chains in the UK, said pressures included higher fuel prices, which have been pushed up by the US-Israeli war on Iran which has effectively stopped tanker traffic through the strait of Hormuz.
Overall, JD said like-for-like sales fell by 3.1% in the second quarter, with its North America operations taking the biggest hit, down by 6.8%. Sales across Europe were down 2.7%.
The UK was a rare bright spot as World Cup excitement drove sales of football replica kits, while consumers bought more outdoor gear, including from its high street brands Blacks and Go Outdoors.
after newsletter promotion
Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at the investment firm Wealth Club, said: “JD Sports is offering another glimpse of the darkening clouds gathering over the US economy, with American shoppers looking considerably more cautious.
“The sneaker is fast becoming a canary in the coalmine for confidence. More consumers are resisting the lure of hyped brands, which is not surprising when the jobs market is weakening and inflation is still such a concern. Consumers may still be spending, but they are becoming more selective about discretionary purchases, particularly when household budgets are already under pressure.”
1040d48b1f6da54005a3a79b.summary: Sports fashion retailer JD Sports has cut its full-year profit forecasts after falling trainer sales, driven by inflation and cost of living pressures. The company reported a 3.1% drop in like-for-like sales for the second quarter, with North America experiencing the steepest decline at 6.8%. Chief executive Régis Schultz noted that tough trading conditions forced the retailer to cut prices and offer promotions.
key_points: JD Sports lowered its full-year pre-tax profit forecast to between £700m and £800m.
Company shares dropped by 12% following the profit warning announcement.
North America saw the largest sales decline at 6.8%, while the UK benefited from World Cup excitement and outdoor gear sales.
Rising fuel prices linked to the conflict involving Iran and the US added to consumer cost of living pressures.

5a239331821bc16aadbd3aa9.title: 'I Don't Understand If It's Such a Big Issue': Shuhei Yoshida Isn't Too Bothered About No More Discs
5a239331821bc16aadbd3aa9.author: Push Square; Stephen Tailby
5a239331821bc16aadbd3aa9.content:
He adds that physical and special editions of games will likely still be released, so those who want something tangible will probably be able to buy them at retail — they'll just contain a PS Store code rather than a disc.
As far as Yoshida is concerned, however, the disc itself is fast becoming redundant in the digital age.
"Even with physical disc games, in most cases, developers are constantly updating and adding game data anyway. Anyone who chooses to purchase a physical version will still need to download new patches, DLC, or updates. So, not having a disc, I don't understand if it’s such a big issue."
It's a fair point, though not completely accurate. Many games you can buy on disc do not in fact require any updates, and will work as soon as you slot them into your console.
Obviously, that's not the case for every game; some do necessitate an online connection, while others are incomplete or perhaps even not on the disc at all, requiring a download to play.
The issue isn't straightforward, and Yoshida's thoughts don't account for everything; there's the small matter of digital games never truly belonging to you, for example.
Anyway, it's always interesting to hear his perspective as someone who's been in the business for such a long time.
5a239331821bc16aadbd3aa9.summary: Shuhei Yoshida believes that physical discs are becoming redundant in the digital age because modern games frequently require downloads, patches, and updates regardless of format. He notes that physical and special editions will likely survive by containing digital store codes instead of discs for those who want tangible items. However, some games can still be played directly from a disc without updates, and digital purchases raise concerns about true ownership.
key_points: Shuhei Yoshida views physical game discs as increasingly redundant.
Physical editions may transition to offering digital store codes.
Many modern physical games still require downloads, patches, and updates.
Some physical games can be played immediately without any updates.
Digital game purchases do not grant the same sense of ownership as physical items.

c1c4f6de7a91972118d0236c.title: Rob Rinder announces dad’s death aged 73 after being diagnosed with illness
c1c4f6de7a91972118d0236c.author: Milo Pope
c1c4f6de7a91972118d0236c.content:
![](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEC_308884273-cc6a.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
Rob Rinder has revealed that his dad has died at the age of 73 after being diagnosed with an illness that has been ‘desperately under-researched’.
The author, TV judge and criminal barrister, shared the news with his followers that David Rinder, who worked as a London black cab driver for over 40 years, has died.
David had been living with Lewy body dementia, leading Rob to become a vocal patron and advocate for the Lewy Body Society to raise awareness for the condition.
Writing on Instagram, Rob wrote: ‘My dad died yesterday aged 73. I wasn’t sure whether to share this but if it brings attention to an illness too few people understand, perhaps it belongs here.
‘A London cabbie & lifelong Spurs supporter, he was there for every one of my brothers’ and grandsons’ football matches. I once represented him at the Carriage Office for bad driving; I loved him but the prosecution had a case…’
Rob, who is also known for his work presenting documentaries and co-hosting travel shows with Rylan Clark, said that his parents divorced when he was young, so he did not grow up with his dad at home.
![](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/GettyImages-497910810-2067-e1777736062989.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
‘We were very different men. I loved opera and all its drama; he loved Tottenham and cigarettes. We both took people as we found them and we both loved women, though in rather different ways.
‘I never once doubted his pride in me. When I came out he responded with magnificent indifference: I was still his son, there was nothing else to discuss.’
Rob praised the work of Jewish Care which became his dad’s home and ‘a place where dignity and tenderness were practised every day’.
‘A Jewish man, held in his final days by people of different faiths: a quiet reminder that what is sacred in us is also what we share. He died with his family around him loved and held to the last,’ he added.
What is Lewy Body dementia?
Lewy body dementia is a type of progressive dementia that causes trouble with thinking, movement, sleep and behaviour.
Sharing symptoms with both Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s, the brain disease is caused by abnormal deposits of a protein called alpha-synuclein building up in the brain. These deposits are called Lewy bodies.
One of the biggest differences between Alzheimer’s and Lewy Body dementia is that memory loss isn’t always the first or most prominent symptom.
With the former, problems with attention, alertness, visual perception and movement can appear early, while memory can fluctuate.
‘Funny, beautifully flawed, loving and my dad. Lewy body dementia took him far too young.
-

(Photo by Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images)](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308618092-8d8c.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646&h=363&crop=1)

‘At least one in ten people living with dementia has Lewy body’s, around 125,000 people in the UK yet it remains poorly understood, frequently missed & desperately under-researched. Please learn its name, learn its signs and if you can support the work to change that.’
Writing in the comments section of his post, Alan Carr and Angela Scanlon offered their condolences to the Judge Rinder star.

b9d681b6eb640e6c3053846c.title: Wright reveals Arsenal transfer worry after Lewis-Skelly exit rumours
b9d681b6eb640e6c3053846c.author: Arthur Ferridge
b9d681b6eb640e6c3053846c.content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Mikel Arteta calls on Arsenal to build momentum after Community Shield victory over Manchester City](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/20/7/38/Ian-Wright-on-The-Overlap.png?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![Arsenal Football Newsletter](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_arsenal_embed_desktop.png)
Standard Sport reported last week that the player had been offered to Chelsea and Manchester United by intermediaries, casting doubt over his future with the Gunners, where he has played since he was eight years old.
No concrete interest seemed to materialise from the rumours, and Lewis-Skelly has impressed in performances against Manchester City and Como since, suggesting he is prepared to stay and fight for his place.
The emergence of those reports, though, has left Wright concerned about Arsenal’s transfer strategy. Speaking on the Stick to Football podcast, he questioned the Gunners’ approach to the market.
“I don’t know where that’s coming from because I know for a fact that’s not coming from his team,” he began. “It’s not coming from his mum. Arsenal fans need to chill out with his mum saying that she’s touting him about.
“Myles has already said he’s happy to say. Why have Arsenal not just said he’s not for sale? He’d be a great signing for Manchester United, of course he would. Look what he’s doing.
“There’s things happening and this again is what I’m worried about with Arsenal, it’s the way we’re doing business with intermediaries now. How’s that story happening when we know for a fact they’re happening and want to stay and are happy.
“Martinelli has not been contacted by anybody at the club but has been touted about everywhere. Who is doing that? Why is that happening?”
Wright went on, questioning the state of Arsenal’s finances as he pointed out the club may be pushed to sell for pure profit.
“The unfortunate thing you get when you’ve got a player who comes through the academy and breaks into the first team and does what they do, you’ve always got that noose of pure profit on them.
Read More
“When you’ve got someone like Myles who is playing well, it’s unbelievable what he’s capable of doing then of course Manchester United will see if something can happen.
“They’ve seen Guimaraes come in; they’ve seen Declan Rice. He doesn’t want to leave and that’s the thing that’s really baffling me is why Arsenal don’t just come in and say he’s not for sale.”
b9d681b6eb640e6c3053846c.summary: Former Arsenal player Ian Wright has raised concerns over Arsenal's business dealings with intermediaries following rumours that young academy product Myles Lewis-Skelly was offered to rival clubs. Despite the player being happy to stay, Wright questioned why the club has not publicly declared him not for sale. He also expressed worry that the pressure for pure profit from academy players could lead to unwanted transfers.
key_points: Intermediaries reportedly offered Myles Lewis-Skelly to Chelsea and Manchester United.
Ian Wright criticized Arsenal's handling of business with intermediaries on the Stick to Football podcast.
Wright questioned why Arsenal did not simply state that the player is not for sale.
Concerns were raised about the financial pressure to sell academy graduates for pure profit.

0740c85b96299d35540fc7a5.title: NASA calls off mission to rescue the falling Swift observatory - Engadget
0740c85b96299d35540fc7a5.author: Mariella Moon
0740c85b96299d35540fc7a5.content:
NASA calls off mission to rescue the falling Swift observatory
Katalyst’s LINK spacecraft will still rendezvous with the telescope but will no longer tug it to a higher orbit.
The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is expected to re-enter and burn up in the Earth's atmosphere later this year, after NASA has aborted the mission meant to tug it back up to a higher orbit. NASA has announced that Katalyst Space's LINK spacecraft will no longer dock with the satellite and boost it to a higher altitude as planned. The agency blamed it on LINK's ongoing attitude control issue, which started in late July.
If you'll recall, NASA reported at the time that the spacecraft was having problems managing its orientation in orbit, causing it to spin helplessly. That led to sporadic communications with the spacecraft. There was also some loss in functionality to LINK's thruster system. NASA and Katalyst were still optimistic last month that the spacecraft could accomplish its goal, but things have clearly changed since then.
Katalyst had less than a year to design a spacecraft for the Swift Boost mission, which launched in early July. Shawn Domagal-Goldman, the Astrophysics Division director at NASA Headquarters in Washington, said it was a "high-risk, high-reward mission" mission from the start. It was a first-of-its-kind attempt, and the team had very little time to try and rescue the Swift telescope, whose orbit is rapidly decaying due to an increase in solar activity in recent years.
NASA's SWIFT observatory launched in 2004 to study gamma ray bursts, but astronomers are now using it for several other purposes. The agency has been relying on it to obtain critical information quickly when a sudden cosmic event takes places. This mission was supposed to add a decade or so to its life. Going forward, NASA says it will prioritize finding "new options to react rapidly to cosmic events," but it will use current missions to help fill the gap for now.
While LINK will no longer tug the Swift observatory to a higher orbit, it will still attempt to rendezvous with it. NASA and Katalyst plan to gather as much data as possible from the rendezvous operations to serve future satellite servicing missions.
"This is not the outcome we were working toward, but it does not change why this mission was worth attempting," said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. "The team moved with extraordinary speed to give Swift a chance to carry out more science while advancing capabilities America will need for satellite servicing in the future. We are going to learn everything we can from LINK's rendezvous attempt and put those lessons to work on the missions that follow."
0740c85b96299d35540fc7a5.summary: NASA has called off a mission to rescue the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory by boosting it to a higher orbit, and the satellite is now expected to burn up in the Earth's atmosphere later this year. The decision follows ongoing attitude control and thruster issues with Katalyst Space's LINK spacecraft, which was designed and launched in July for the high-risk rescue attempt. Although the docking and tugging portion of the mission is canceled, the LINK spacecraft will still attempt to rendezvous with the telescope to gather valuable data for future satellite servicing.
key_points: NASA has canceled the mission to rescue and re-boost the falling Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory.
The cancellation is due to ongoing attitude control and thruster problems experienced by Katalyst Space's LINK spacecraft since July.
The Swift observatory, which launched in 2004, is now expected to re-enter and burn up in Earth's atmosphere later this year.
Despite calling off the orbit boost, the LINK spacecraft will still attempt to rendezvous with Swift to collect data for future satellite missions.
NASA will now prioritize finding new ways to react rapidly to cosmic events while using existing missions to fill the gap.

c5831006cd482ed23719a706.title: York warned of salmonella outbreak after person dies and hundreds affected
c5831006cd482ed23719a706.author: Abby Backhouse
c5831006cd482ed23719a706.content:
PEOPLE in York have been warned after a person has died and hundreds of people have been affected by a salmonella outbreak, health officials have said.
The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said the food poisoning outbreak “may be linked to eggs imported from outside of the UK”.
There has been one death associated with the outbreak, UKHSA said.
RECOMMENDED READING:
The Food Standards Agency (FSA) said that there is “no evidence that UK-produced eggs are affected”.
It said that investigations had identified links to imported eggs “mainly used by food service and catering establishments such as restaurants or cafes, as a potential source”.
Salmonella generally causes a self-limiting gastroenteritis, with symptoms including stomach cramps, diarrhoea, vomiting or fever.
More than a third of people affected (38%) in the outbreak were admitted to hospital, with two people developing potentially life-threatening blood stream infections.
UKHSA said between August 11 last year and August 1 this year, 207 cases have been confirmed – 199 in England, six in Scotland, one in Wales and one in Northern Ireland.
One expert said that the figure reported “is likely to be just the tip of the iceberg” as many cases will be unreported.
The regions in England with the highest number of cases are London, where 47 cases were confirmed, and Yorkshire and Humber (38).
People affected include babies and people as old as 90, according to the UKHSA.
Hannah Charles, lead epidemiologist for gastrointestinal infections at UKHSA, said: “We’re working with Food Standards Agency and other public health agencies to investigate a salmonella outbreak that may be linked to eggs imported from outside of the UK.
“Salmonellosis is often caused by eating or handling contaminated food and can be spread rarely from person-to-person.
“Salmonella generally causes a mild illness, although vulnerable groups with weakened immune systems may experience more severe illness.
“Symptoms of a salmonella infection include diarrhoea, stomach cramps and sometimes vomiting and fever. Anyone who is concerned about symptoms should contact their GP or out of hours service in the first instance.
“There are simple steps to prevent the spread of salmonella: wash your hands thoroughly after using the bathroom and before preparing and handling food, cook food thoroughly, and if you have any symptoms, avoid handling food for others where possible.”
Jacquelyn McCormick, head of incidents at the Food Standards Agency, said: “We are working closely with the UK Health Security Agency and other partners to investigate an outbreak of Salmonella Enteritidis.
“The exact cause has not yet been identified, however investigations so far have identified links to eggs imported from outside the UK, mainly used by food service and catering establishments such as restaurants or cafes, as a potential source.
“There is no evidence that UK-produced eggs are affected.
“While investigations continue, our advice around eating eggs remains the same. Eggs which are thoroughly cooked and handled hygienically should not present a food safety risk.
“Infants, young children, pregnant people and older adults should only eat runny or raw eggs if they have a British Lion mark or are produced under the Laid in Britain egg assurance scheme.
“This advice does not apply to those who are severely immunocompromised and require medically supervised diets.
“We continue to advise people who are handling eggs, eggshells or egg packaging to always wash their hands thoroughly with warm water and soap and dry them properly afterwards.”
Dr Damien Tully, associate professor at the Medical Research Council/Uganda Virus Research Institute and London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine Uganda Research Unit, said: “This is a sizeable outbreak, but the number of confirmed cases is likely to be just the tip of the iceberg.
“Many salmonella infections cause relatively short-lived gastrointestinal illness and people may recover without ever being tested, meaning the true number of infections associated with an outbreak can be considerably higher than the number identified through laboratory surveillance.”
Dr Tully added: “For most healthy people, salmonella causes an unpleasant but self-limiting illness, although it can occasionally cause serious disease, particularly in young children, older adults and people with weakened immune systems.
“Good food hygiene remains important: wash your hands before preparing or eating food, avoid cross-contamination in the kitchen, and make sure foods such as eggs, poultry and meat are cooked thoroughly.”
Nick Allen, chief executive of the British Egg Industry Council, said: “It is deeply concerning that imported eggs are once again under scrutiny in connection with a serious salmonella outbreak.

PEOPLE in York have been warned after a person has died and hundreds of people have been affected by a salmonella outbreak, health officials have said.
The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said the food poisoning outbreak “may be linked to eggs imported from outside of the UK”.
There has been one death associated with the outbreak, UKHSA said.

The Food Standards Agency (FSA) said that there is “no evidence that UK-produced eggs are affected”.
It said that investigations had identified links to imported eggs “mainly used by food service and catering establishments such as restaurants or cafes, as a potential source”.
Salmonella generally causes a self-limiting gastroenteritis, with symptoms including stomach cramps, diarrhoea, vomiting or fever.
More than a third of people affected (38%) in the outbreak were admitted to hospital, with two people developing potentially life-threatening blood stream infections.
UKHSA said between August 11 last year and August 1 this year, 207 cases have been confirmed – 199 in England, six in Scotland, one in Wales and one in Northern Ireland.
One expert said that the figure reported “is likely to be just the tip of the iceberg” as many cases will be unreported.
The regions in England with the highest number of cases are London, where 47 cases were confirmed, and Yorkshire and Humber (38).
People affected include babies and people as old as 90, according to the UKHSA.

“Salmonellosis is often caused by eating or handling contaminated food and can be spread rarely from person-to-person.
“Salmonella generally causes a mild illness, although vulnerable groups with weakened immune systems may experience more severe illness.
“Symptoms of a salmonella infection include diarrhoea, stomach cramps and sometimes vomiting and fever. Anyone who is concerned about symptoms should contact their GP or out of hours service in the first instance.
“There are simple steps to prevent the spread of salmonella: wash your hands thoroughly after using the bathroom and before preparing and handling food, cook food thoroughly, and if you have any symptoms, avoid handling food for others where possible.”
Jacquelyn McCormick, head of incidents at the Food Standards Agency, said: “We are working closely with the UK Health Security Agency and other partners to investigate an outbreak of Salmonella Enteritidis.
“The exact cause has not yet been identified, however investigations so far have identified links to eggs imported from outside the UK, mainly used by food service and catering establishments such as restaurants or cafes, as a potential source.

“Good food hygiene remains important: wash your hands before preparing or eating food, avoid cross-contamination in the kitchen, and make sure foods such as eggs, poultry and meat are cooked thoroughly.”

b7c1849fad0da9acbffac25b.title: The 6 best free things to do in London this weekend [August 21-23 2026]
b7c1849fad0da9acbffac25b.author: Alice Saville
b7c1849fad0da9acbffac25b.content:
[title]
There are a billion and one different things to do in London over the summer. Day festivals, bars, outdoor theatre shows and blockbuster exhibitions are all jostling for attention and competing for your time, and cash. But what happens when September is looming, and your bank account is looking drier than one of Hackney’s drought-stricken canals?
Well, we’ve got an idea or two. We’ve hunted high and low across this city to find free things to do this weekend that are actually worth your time. Spectacular circus acts in the open air. Queer dance parties with the edgiest DJs around. Joyful street parties with live music. Don’t let the fun run out when the funds run out. Read on for our pick of the very best events to enjoy, without getting your bankcard out.
The best free things on in London this weekend, August 21-23 2026
In a city where free theatre is harder to come by than an outdoor table at Towpath Cafe, Greenwich Fair is an annual miracle. It takes over the summit of Greenwich Park for a weekend of outdoor shows that play across multiple stages, with roving performers working the crowd. No need to book: just turn up, find a seat, and discover anything from feminist high-wire act ElevateHer by Daughters of the Wire, to Kismat Walla by Thingumajig Theatre, a magical outdoor puppetry show inspired by South Asian street markets.
Greenwich Park, Park Row, SE10 8XJ. Sat Aug 22 - Sun Aug 23. Free.
![Caspian’s Storm, Greenwich Fair, 2026](https://media.timeout.com/images/106426191/image.webp) 
It’s been a big old summer of LGBTQ+ partying, with Pride, Mighty Hoopla, and Body Movements all pulling fun-loving crowds of revellers. Now, it’s time to head east and enjoy one of the last massive get-togethers of this year’s queer calendar: and thankfully for everyone’s bank balance, it’s totally free. Queer Frequencies is the latest in the series of free parties that began with The Music Is Ours back in June. It’s a party that’ll put Black queer music and culture front and centre , with a line-up curated by DJ Shy One, ‘the Prince of Peckham’ Mark-Ashley Dupé, east London creative Donnie Sunshine and DJ Joel Mignott. Head on over to Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park for an afternoon of dancing and discovering new acts in the late August sunshine.
Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, E20 2ST. Sat Aug 22 - Sun Aug 23. Free.
Arts Emergency is a charity that’s dedicated to making sure the next generation of creatives find their way into the spotlight, even as schools cut art, music, theatre and literature out of the curriculum. Get a feel for what they do at this exciting two-day takeover at Southbank Centre. On Saturday, you’ll find loads of ways to get moving, with workshops by dance groups Strut, Queer Salsa, and Polyjammerous. Then on Sunday, there’s a one-off edition of storytelling open mic night Special Guest, where actors, writers and comedians tell stories inspired by words from the audience, backed up by a live band.
Southbank Centre, Belvedere Road, SE1 8XX. Sat Aug 22 - Sun Aug 23. Free.
![Pinterest](https://media.timeout.com/images/106437371/image.webp) 
Delight your friends and befuddle your enemies by getting some sparkling face gems at Pinterest’s Mile End pop-up, which is all about getting festival-ready. You’ll also be able to pick up e.l.f. cosmetics and learn how to use them from the pros, as well as getting your mitts on customisable single use cameras and festival merch. And if the ‘festival’ you’re going to is your very un-Pinterest-worthy disposable BBQ in your mate’s arid backyard? Don't worry, we won’t tell ‘em if you don’t.
All Time Food and Wine, 564 Mile End Road, E3 4PH. Sat Aug 22. Free.
Ridley Road Market is never quiet, but this Saturday it’s going to be buzzing to a different frequency thanks to its annual summer party. From noon, it’ll be soundtracked by the sweet sounds of steel pan bands, sound systems and African drumming workshops. There’ll also be face painting for the kids, a free photobooth, fun interactive games to try – and of course, loads of delicious food from Ridley Road’s many traders.
Ridley Road Market, E8. Sat Aug 22. Free.
![Buzz Gym’s Soca dance class](https://media.timeout.com/images/106438448/image.webp) 
Bored of punishing 5k runs or tedious weight-training? Try a fun new form of exercise at this free Wembley Park workshop, which will introduce you to the joys of Caribbean Soca dancing. Buzz Gym will lead you through an hour of fast-paced, rhythmic movement that'll send you beaming into the rest of your Sunday.
Union Park, Wembley Park. Sun Aug 23. Free.
Make the most of August with our guide to the best things to do in London this month.
Get the latest and greatest from the Big Smoke – from news and reviews to events and trends. Just follow our Time Out London WhatsApp channel.
Stay in the loop: sign up for our free Time Out London newsletter for the best of the city, straight to your inbox.
b7c1849fad0da9acbffac25b.summary: London offers several free events and activities for the weekend of August 21-23, 2026, helping residents enjoy the city despite diminishing summer funds. Highlights include outdoor circus performances at Greenwich Park, a Black queer music party at Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, and a two-day creative takeover at the Southbank Centre. Additional free experiences feature a festival pop-up in Mile End, a lively summer party at Ridley Road Market, and a Soca dance class in Wembley Park.

Queer Frequencies hosts a free celebration of Black queer music and culture at Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park.
The Southbank Centre hosts a two-day Arts Emergency takeover with dance workshops and a storytelling open mic night.
Pinterest and e.l.f. cosmetics are running a free festival-ready pop-up at Mile End on Saturday, August 22.
Ridley Road Market's annual summer party offers steel pan bands, African drumming, and games on Saturday, August 22.

a1cfe830abd990298b30c7ae.title: Burnham says fly-tippers will be forced to pay for the clean-up when they dump waste illegally – UK politics live
a1cfe830abd990298b30c7ae.author: Tom Ambrose; Vivian Ho; Kiran Stacey; Aletha Adu; Caroline Davies; Rowena Mason
a1cfe830abd990298b30c7ae.content:
National Crime Agency brought in to tackle organised gangs behind illegal dumps
Andy Burnham has said fly-tippers will be forced to pay for the clean-up when they dump waste illegally.
The prime minister laid out his plans to crackdown on waste crimes as he visited an illegal dump in West Yorkshire.
He told broadcasters:
We’ve begun a much more networked approach to this, where we’re bringing the National Crime Agency in to work with the Environment Agency, increasing the penalties and bearing down now on the organised crime that lies behind some of what you see behind me.
Asked why the National Crime Agency was involved, the prime minister said:
It’s building the intelligence as to who is behind this, the networks that are orchestrating what is a very serious crime, and then using the Proceeds of Crime Act to make them pay for the clean-up.
It cannot be right that we leave the situation to build, the public purse then exposed in relation to the clean-up.
But actually we should be getting in much earlier, apprehending them, using all of the intelligence that comes through that investigation to make sure the polluter pays.
Racism and sexism have become normalised in Britain, the equalities minister has said, as she warned that young men were being sucked into violent misogyny by the “cesspit” of social media.
Bridget Phillipson said she was increasingly worried about how commonplace misogyny and racism had become, fuelled by online interactions and statements by politicians she said would not have been acceptable a few years ago.
She accused senior MPs from Reform and the Conservatives of having made racist statements in recent years, and accused the police of not taking violence against women and girls seriously enough.
Speaking to the Guardian’s Politics Weekly podcast, she said: “I worry that we are at kind of a ground zero in terms of attitudes around violence against women and girls.
“Things that not very long ago felt totally unacceptable are becoming normal. I think we’re seeing that in terms of attitudes towards women, and I think we see that in terms of attitudes around racism.”
She accused the shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, and Reform’s economic spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, of having made racist statements in recent years.
Bridget Phillipson has suggested her sweeping reforms to special educational needs provision could be adapted to give parents greater protections if they are unhappy about the service being provided for their children.
The former education secretary told the Guardian ministers were open to making changes to the plans, which were announced earlier this year but which have since been subject to consultation.
Under Andy Burnham, Phillipson has been moved to the women and equalities brief, but she said that before she left the education department the plan had been to make moderations to the plans after the consultation process.
Parents and some MPs have particularly expressed concern that under the new system, parents who are denied an Education, Health and Care Plan (EHCP) will not be able to demand that local authorities move their child to a particular school.
Phillipson said however that some of the legal protections in the new system could be strengthened to give parents more confidence.
“The consultation was a genuine one and, you know, final decisions are still to be taken,” she told the Guardian’s Politics Weekly podcast.
“I do obviously recognise the enormous kind of nervousness that many parents will be experiencing if their children are in that system,” she said.
And she added: “I can only speak to where I kind of left things … It was clear to me through the passage of that consultation, through the events we did right across the country, hearing directly from parents, through all of the conversations I had, that there were areas where there would need to be more finessing of some aspects of the policy.”
Labour MP for Bradford West Naz Shar and Environment Agency staff show Andy Burnham an illegal rubbish dump near Bradford City’s football ground.
Labour MP for Bradford West Naz Shar (L), and Environment agency staff show Britain's prime minister Andy Burnham (C), an illegal rubbish dump near the Bradford City football ground in Bradford, northern England on 20 August 2026. Photograph: Scott Heppell/AFP/Getty Images
Education Lucy Powell on Thursday addressed the GCSE gender gap, which shrank to its narrowest point this century.
Almost one in four boys in England received top grades in maths while results in English improved across the board.
“The white working-class review that was recently done, that was one things it found, that more boys need to see the purpose of education, they need to see the line of sight into work,” Powell told the Press Association.
“I just spoke today here at Harper Green to some young lads doing the construction qualification they’ve now put on here, and that’s exactly what they said to me, is that they feel it’s engaging, they understand the purpose of it, they want to use their hands and their skills in different ways.
“So that’s giving them a reason to come to school and then they’ll engage in the other subjects as well.”
Andy Burnham told reporters that funding for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s security arrangements on their return to the UK was a “private matter”.
Harry and Meghan are expected to return to live in Britain later this month. After six years in the US, they will be moving with their two children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, to a non-royal residence outside of London.
After stepping down as senior royals, the Sussexes are no longer eligible to receive taxpayer-funded protection while in the UK, other than when within royal residences. Prince Harry, 41, has previously stated that he would not feel safe bringing his family back to the UK without police protection.
When questioned about their security arrangements, the prime minister said: “Well, this is a private matter.
“It’s a matter for Harry and for Meghan, and we wish them well in the moves that they’re making.”
The Guardian’s Rowena Mason has more on Richard Tice, business spokesperson for Reform UK, and his defence of the party’s decision to suspendTimMontgomerie:
Reform UK has been stalling in the polls in recent months following questions about Nigel Farage’s financial affairs, with a personal £5m gift from Thailand-based billionaire Christopher Harborne currently under investigation by parliament’s standards watchdog.
The party has also faced splits over the actions of Zia Yusuf, its home affairs spokesperson, who branded a senior Tory a “traitor”, and the decision to suspend Tim Montgomerie, a high profile activist who had defected from the Conservatives.
Montgomerie had been critical of Farage’s decision not to attend the count when he won the Clacton byelection, and said the leader had show a “too dominant aggrieved tone”, arguing that “you don’t skip your own victory count without a much better explanation”.
The Reform member, who had posed with Farage when he joined the party, was informed earlier this week of his suspension.
Asked at a press conference whether the party had become too thin skinned and unable to take criticism, Tice said it was “far from” the case and Reform was beginning to climb again in the polls.
He added: “We’re not afraid of competition, voters have got more choice and none of us have ever claimed we are perfect … we get lots right, we make mistakes, we push on.”
National Crime Agency brought in to tackle organised gangs behind illegal dumps
